en: With a thimble mouth and camel-calf eyes,
Too restless to remain in anyone's grasp,
Gracious and knowing how to show respect,
Unlike ordinary women,
One surpassingly cheerful and capable—
From those your sister-in-law chose one.
With a thimble mouth and desirous eyes,
Who, when she saw a young man,
Spoke all manner of yearning words,
From such women she chose one.
With a chest like a running hunting hound,
And eyes like a coursing hound,
With a graceful neck and camel-calf eyes,
From these she chose one.
One whose sight opened the heart,
A renowned beauty with a moon-bright face,
From those fine women she chose one.
Broad-lunged and breathing heavily,
With a hanging dewlap and a thick neck,
Able to load the tent securely,
And draw the ropes tight,
An outstanding woman among women,
A wrestler who moved with heavy thuds—
From these she chose one.
With breasts showing upon her chest,
Whose sight opened a person's heart,
From these she chose one.
From those who bound their hair with yellow gold
And braided it in wondrous fashion,
She chose one.
From accomplished women who had spent much time
In the company of young men,
Who, before one could say this or that,
In the time it took to open and close one's eyes,
Could finish any task,
From those she chose one.
From cheerful women of strong character,
From the accomplished and unashamed,
She chose one.
One who had matured like a doe,
Whose hair wound around her feet,
Who had matured like a red deer,
Whose hair wound around her head—
She took a sensible leader.
She took surpassingly beautiful young women,
And skilled, graceful women from among the brides;
She took a maiden more beautiful
Than all the other young women.
Into the valley of Opol Mountain,
Beside Great Urgench,
They gathered to play their games.
The poor woman longed deeply
To go out and welcome her lord.
So that not a single person could leave,
She had the mouth of the gate sealed.
When her mother came trembling,
And stood shrieking to bar her daughters,
Saying, "Do not go,"
Churok mocked her mother.
Broad river valley, spring, and sheer cliff—
The graceful, black-eyed beauty,
Proud Churok, poor woman.
The tent with golden edging
Khan Akun's treasury—
Within that treasury,
Within the treasury she had sixty folded,
And loaded upon white camels.
Saying, "Let my mighty lord eat,"
She brought countless kinds of cooked food;
Saying, "Let him drink until his thirst is quenched,"
She brought liquor distilled from raisins,
Grain cooked in cream,
And costly tea for drinking.
She took a barren three-year-old horse for slaughter,
Leading the horse loose and untethered.
To render service,
From the renowned city of Afghanistan
She took sixty young men as attendants.
The campsite where they arrived and dismounted
Was in the hollow of Ak-Kyya,
Beside Great Urgench.
Delighting all who looked,
Upon the blue-green meadow grass
She had sixty carpets
Of surpassing quality spread out.
Such was the nature of those carpets:
If they soaked in water for forty years,
Not even their edges would fade;
If cast in water for eighty years,
They would not soften and rot.
Their sight opened the heart.
When she took some sixty carpets
And had them spread,
The likeness of paradise appeared.
At the sight, the poor man faltered,
And the gray wolf's heart opened.
Churok, daughter of Akun,
Appeared like a noble maiden.
Before your lord's eyes
Speckled flies seemed to dance;
Words spoken early seemed to become late.
To join in embrace with Churok,
The daughter of Akun,
To reach her there at once,
The lion lord Semetey
Stared with all four eyes.
Fully satisfying the heart,
Of satin and silk quilts
That Churok had sixty
Laid in ordered rows.
Saying, "If his ardor rises, he may put it on,"
She had bulletproof plate armor
Covered in splendid fashion.
Poor, fierce Aychurok
Had some sixty tents
Raised in a wondrous row.
If a young man did not go there in desire,
It was as though his hearth-fire had died.
When one looked at every contour of her body,
This Churok, daughter of Akun,
Was like a demon moving at dusk.
When your lord looked at an angle,
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Poured out and began their games.
In their midst Aychurok
Appeared in the form of the morning star.
Even milk and fermented cream seemed amazed,
Saying, "Can a mortal be like this?"
And the hero's heart opened.
The poor, serene woman's
Manner appeared wondrous.
She walked with a long, radiant stride;
Sixty buttons and forty clasps
Upon the difficult beauty's
Breast glittered brightly.
A body amulet of yellow gold,
Its cord showed at her throat.
The broad-chested lord's
Mind was deeply distracted.
Akun Khan was a khan renowned among the people;
The full-figured unfortunate woman
Had the tail feathers of a parrot
Set in ninety different arrangements
Upon her blue lynx-fur hat.
Behold the wisdom of Churok,
And the turmoil so openly born.
Amid thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Stood Aychurok;
Beside the great flowing river
They gathered and began their games.
When your great lord, fierce by birth,
Saw Aychurok,
He nearly dropped dead.
Taking his spyglass in his hand,
From the ridge of Acha-Tash
He shouted in fury,
Calling by name for his young men,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro.
That poor lion who could not be stirred
Was now a poor hero ready to move.
When they heard his shout,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro
Bent their knees toward the ground.
Without delay, to learn the news,
And to reach their lord,
They put on their arms and armor.
Flying like arrows, the young men
Made ready their several mounts.
The horse one companion rode
Was Kokburchak of Kobosh Khan;
The horse the other companion rode
Was Abyke's Aktelki.
They vaulted on like shepherds,
And rode before the face
Of the wrathful Bloodthirsty One.
Racing until they drew even,
The young men conferred:
"Our khan-slaying elder is a tiger;
His cry rang out loudly.
His cry was terribly harsh
And seemed to devour our ears and noses.
There is haste and alarm
In our elder's voice.
Is there a deeply dug trench?
Is there an army raising an uproar?
Is there a trench dug deep?
Has some formidable enemy
Surrounded him on every side?
Our lord's voice rang loud.
Has something borne down upon his head?
Has our gray-wolf lord taken fright?
If an unceasing clamor has arisen,
If a merciless uproar has broken out,
If a grim, deep-browed foe appears,
If an enemy comes crying havoc,
Let us reach the hero
And crush the danger utterly;
Let us free and recover
The hero-born gray wolf!
If the enemy has come from Mecca,
Let us choose and mount the finest coursers,
Scatter all of them,
And drive them toward their homeland.
If the enemy has come from China,
Let us drive them back into Kakan."
Having settled it thus, the young men
Raced toward their elder;
Their two stirrups struck together.
Spurring in breathless haste,
They turned their horses' heads.
When they reached their elder,
They took their spears in hand;
The companions of fearsome bearing
Stood bristling and alert.
When the young men arrived and stood there,
The young lord Semetey,
As though his fierce mother Kanykey
Had given birth to a man indeed,
Smiled and beamed broadly,
His shovel-broad teeth gleaming,
His mail coat glittering upon him,
Your sovereign lord began to speak:
"Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
My matched pair of companions!
My cliff that even geese cannot circle,
My deeds before God must have been pure
For my God to give me you two.
My matched pair of companions,
Keep these words in mind:
Today I have seen a wonder.
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You are the morning stars above my head,
The costly beaver at my collar.
When I send you ahead, you are my open road;
When I place you behind, you are my countless host.
You are those I fondle and love,
Those who wear my bulletproof coat;
When an army comes covering the earth,
When force threatens my fly-sized soul,
You enter battle without a start!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
When you were infant children,
So that you would become stout-hearted heroes,
I had you fed slices of kazy;
So that you would be my own brothers,
I had both of you nurse
At Kanykey's breast!
You and your companion
Kicked each other like yearling colts
And nursed in rivalry at her breast.
My courser fit for a six-month ride,
The sustaining shadow of a toiling soul,
My dear kinsmen, let me cherish you!
Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
You possess a noble nature that commands the gaze;
You are vigorous legacies left to me
